note:
CHIEF COMPLAINT
Difficulty swallowing with chest pain for several weeks.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Patient is a male presenting with dysphagia and chest pain upon swallowing over the past several weeks. He reports that the pain occurs most of the time when swallowing, particularly with larger pieces of food that feel like they are getting stuck. He denies weight loss and reports actually gaining weight over this period. He has been under stress due to a recent move from the West Coast to the East Coast over the last couple of months, during which time his diet has consisted of pizza, burgers, and other heavy foods. He has occasional epigastric pain but denies abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. He denies hematochezia or melena.

REVIEW OF SYSTEMS
Denies fever, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea. Reports occasional epigastric discomfort. Denies blood in stool or dark tarry stools. No other systemic symptoms reported.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY
Not provided in visit.

MEDICATIONS
Not provided in visit.

ALLERGIES
Not provided in visit.

FAMILY HISTORY
Not provided in visit.

SOCIAL HISTORY
Patient recently relocated from West Coast to East Coast due to dissatisfaction with West Coast living. Reports significant stress related to the move and concern about transporting his dog. Currently eating foods high in fat and processed items (pizza, burgers). Denies specific alcohol and caffeine use but doctor counseled on these.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
Vital Signs: BP 133/70, HR normal, afebrile, O2 sat 100%, RR 19, weight gain of approximately 10 pounds over the past month noted.
General: No obvious ulcers or evidence of thrush in oral cavity. Tonsils midline. Neck without adenopathy or thyromegaly.
Abdomen: Nondistended with active bowel sounds. No tenderness to palpation of epigastric area. Negative Murphy's sign. No peritoneal signs or rebound.
Lungs: Clear to auscultation bilaterally.
Skin: No rash, lesions, or bruising.
Eyes: Equal and reactive to light.

RESULTS
Barium swallow study revealed two areas of mild narrowing in the mid and lower portions of the esophagus consistent with esophagitis.

ASSESSMENT AND PLAN
Acute esophagitis with esophageal narrowing.

Plan:
1. Medication: Protonix 40 mg once daily in the morning and Carafate 1 gram four times daily for one month to reduce acid production and coat the esophageal and gastric lining.
2. Dietary modifications: Decrease alcohol and caffeine intake, avoid citrus fruits and spicy foods until symptoms improve. Eat slowly and chew food thoroughly.
3. Schedule upper endoscopy for next week to rule out other pathology.
4. Follow-up visit next week post-endoscopy.
5. Counseled on lifestyle modifications and importance of healthy eating once settled into new residence.
